result.reading: The answer changes inside the stated ranges: 0.50x the weight at the worst corner (0.03 kg, 0.007 m2, 4.8 m/s) and 3.42x at the best. A design whose own range contains both answers has not been shown to fly; narrow an input and ask again.

lift_coefficient.note: C_Lmax 1.48 is BORROWED: it was measured on live Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider, a marsupial) in free glides, mean angle of attack 44.15 +/- 3.12 deg and is applied here to Mus musculus because the NCBI taxonomy places both inside Theria <mammals>. Measured in a marsupial glider and offered across Theria, which is marsupials and placentals together. For any taxon other than Petaurus breviceps this is a BORROW across a clade, and the check labels it so. It is the closest measurement in this repository to a gliding mammal; it is not a measurement of the animal being designed.
lift_coefficient.caveat: THIS IS A STALLED-MEMBRANE GLIDE COEFFICIENT, NOT A STEADY-FLIGHT MAXIMUM, and the source is explicit that it was not enough. In the same glides the animals accelerated downward at 1.0 +/- 0.5 m/s2 and forward at 2.1 +/- 0.6 m/s2: Bishop states that body weight was NOT fully supported by aerodynamic force and that some of the lift went into forward acceleration. The angles of attack are far above where an engineered wing stalls. Bishop KL 2006 (J Exp Biol 209:689-701, doi 10.1242/jeb.02062) reports the same for Glaucomys volans, gliding at 35.4-53.5 deg with the wings stalled and accelerating downward, and finds flying squirrels reach higher lift coefficients than sugar gliders -- so 1.48 is, if anything, generous for a mammal without a flying squirrel's specialisations.
lift_coefficient.source: Bishop KL 2007, Aerodynamic force generation, performance and control of body orientation during gliding in sugar gliders (Petaurus breviceps), J Exp Biol 210:2593-2606
lift_coefficient.area_convention: the whole outstretched body-and-membrane planform, as digitised from the gliding animal

result.scope: One inequality -- does lift at the stated speed carry the stated weight -- evaluated from inputs the caller declares, with a maximum lift coefficient taken by clade from a named measurement. It is a STEADY-STATE AREA CHECK. It says nothing about powered flight, nothing about control or stability, nothing about whether the animal can produce the speed, and nothing about whether what carries the weight for one second carries it for a minute.
